A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same AFA/SABW research, with matching original methods, experiments and figures. Text, equations and visual material support reliable comparison. V1 ends with references; v2 includes readable Appendices A–O.

before.justification: V1 reports original generation experiments on COCO 2017 and Draw Bench Prompts, including baseline comparisons, ablations, attention visualizations and inference-step analyses.

after.justification: V2 retains those empirical results and adds original MoE comparisons, additional dataset and architecture evaluations, scaling studies, robustness tests and a distillation experiment.

M1.justification: The main AFA/SABW architecture, denoising objective and Algorithm 1 are retained. Appendix K adds an experimental LCM distillation procedure that trains only SABW with frozen denoisers to target fewer inference steps. This unsuccessful variant is a limited procedural addition, not a replacement of AFA.

E1.justification: V1 trains on JourneyDB and evaluates on COCO 2017 and Draw Bench Prompts. V2 adds evaluation on DiffusionDB and LAION-COCO, also evaluates held-out JourneyDB, and trains an additional LAION-COCO variant (Appendices L and N). This substantially broadens the represented data while retaining text-to-image generation as the task.

E2.justification: V2 adds evaluated Denoiser-Level and Block-Level MoE comparators (Tables 4–6). Its reduced-step comparison also adds Weighted Merging, MBW, autoMBW and MagicFusion (Table 8), whereas v1's corresponding Figure 4 compares only base models and AFA. The original comparator sets in Tables 1–2 remain unchanged.

E3.justification: The original training and COCO/Draw Bench protocols are retained, with details moved to Appendix C. New protocols include 0–18,000 training-sample sweeps, ensembles up to six models, timing batches of one/two/four images, SDXL and FLUX configurations, and LCM testing at one/two/four steps. Additional dataset evaluations randomly select 50,000 samples each and exclude training examples from JourneyDB testing.

E4.justification: The original component ablations and attention analyses remain. V2 adds training-size and ensemble-size sensitivity, broader reduced-step comparisons, robustness to correlated low-quality models, training-data-quality controls, and an unsuccessful distillation analysis (Appendices D, G–K, M–N). These investigate substantial additional questions about scalability, robustness and failure conditions.

E5.justification: The existing 20-repeat Draw Bench evaluation is retained; Appendix C newly specifies that averaged metrics are reported. Tables 6 and 9 additionally disclose 20-run timing evaluations. Neither version reports confidence intervals or formal significance tests, and v2 does not establish an increase in the original evaluation run count.

E6.justification: Original Tables 1–3 retain their numerical results. V2 adds substantial benchmark, MoE, scaling, efficiency and robustness results in Tables 4–16 and Figure 8. For example, Table 10 reports AFA IR of 0.6342 versus the best SDXL base model's 0.6339, while Table 11 reports failed four-step LCM distillation with IR −0.5846. These are newly reported settings, not improvements over v1 under unchanged conditions.

T1.justification: Appendix F adds mathematical definitions for the MoE comparators, including router logits, Gumbel-softmax probabilities, straight-through selection and inference routing (Equations 13–20), plus forward-pass complexity reasoning. The original AFA mathematics and denoising-capability definitions remain unchanged; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction contributions and conclusion retain the same central claims: adaptive feature aggregation through SABW, frozen base denoisers, and improved image quality and context alignment. The expanded appendix evidence does not materially redefine these main contributions.

C2.justification: V2 adds explanations of training-data saturation, MoE routing and parallelism tradeoffs, and robustness to correlated models and lower-quality training data. Appendix J qualifies the small gains and practicality of larger backbones, while Appendix K suggests frozen denoisers may explain failed distillation. These substantially expand interpretation and applicability boundaries beyond v1's efficiency discussion.

D1.justification: Beyond v1's optimizer settings, training budget and approximate parameter count, v2 supplies parameter-count breakdowns, MoE implementation equations, new checkpoint links and A6000 timing context. Appendix O discloses eight 32GB V100 GPUs and FP16 memory measurements for two-, three- and six-model ensembles. These are principally additional disclosures, not evidence that the original training setup changed.

R1.justification: Appendix F substantially expands positioning against sparse MoE and timestep-specialized diffusion experts, adding references such as MEME and explaining their differences from ensembling pretrained denoisers. V2 also adds references for LCM, SDXL, DiT, DiffusionDB and recent conditional-generation work. The original merging and MagicFusion positioning is retained.

P1.justification: The main section sequence and most existing prose remain intact. Algorithm 1 and detailed evaluation descriptions move to Appendices A and C, Section 3.3 expands the attention explanation, and author/affiliation text, wording and acknowledgments change. Most additional length comes from new scientific content rather than extensive rewriting.

P2.justification: V2 adopts the ICLR layout, places Tables 1–2 side by side and wraps Table 3 beside the ablation discussion. It corrects Figure 1's reversed cat/dog prompt labels and adds Figures 8–9 and Tables 4–16. The original qualitative image panels are retained.

improvement.justification: V2 substantially addresses v1's limited validation through learned-routing comparisons, broader datasets and backbones, and controlled scaling and robustness studies. Reporting failed distillation, modest gains on stronger models and hardware requirements improves transparency and practical assessment. Uncertainty intervals remain absent, and parameter counts are unreconciled between Appendix B and Table 6, but these limitations do not outweigh the substantial gains in evidence and reproducibility.
